clinicalPearls: The commonest Usher subtype: congenital, non-progressive or slowly progressive moderate-to-severe sensorineural hearing loss with preserved vestibular function.
The hearing loss is characteristically sloping, worse for higher frequencies, so speech is often acquired with hearing aids without needing cochlear implantation.
Normal vestibular function means motor milestones, including walking, are reached at the expected age, distinguishing it from type 1.
Retinitis pigmentosa typically presents later than in type 1, with night blindness often beginning around adolescence or early adulthood.
USH2A, encoding usherin, accounts for the majority of cases; other loci include ADGRV1 (GPR98) and WHRN (whirlin).
USH2A variants are also a frequent cause of non-syndromic autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa, so the same gene spans syndromic and isolated retinal disease.
Hearing aids and communication support usually suffice for auditory rehabilitation, with cochlear implantation reserved for those who progress.
Autosomal recessive inheritance warrants genetic counselling and consideration of retinal gene-specific therapeutic trials.
reference.pathophysiology: Usher syndrome type 2 is an autosomal recessive condition most often caused by biallelic variants in USH2A, which encodes usherin, a very large transmembrane protein; other cases arise from variants in ADGRV1 (an adhesion G-protein-coupled receptor) and WHRN (whirlin). These proteins assemble at the ankle-link region of developing cochlear hair-cell stereocilia and at the periciliary membrane complex of photoreceptors, where they contribute to stereociliary cohesion and to the maintenance of the photoreceptor connecting cilium. Because the encoded proteins are more important for maintenance than for the profound early transduction machinery affected in type 1, cochlear hair-cell dysfunction is partial, giving moderate-to-severe rather than profound deafness, and vestibular hair cells are largely spared, preserving balance. In the retina, gradual failure of periciliary transport and outer-segment turnover produces a rod-predominant then cone degeneration that manifests as retinitis pigmentosa with a characteristically later onset than type 1. The residual function of these proteins therefore explains the milder, later-onset phenotype across both the auditory and visual systems.
additionalDifferentials: Usher syndrome type 1 (profound congenital deafness with vestibular areflexia and earlier retinitis pigmentosa)
Usher syndrome type 3 (progressive postlingual hearing loss)
Non-syndromic autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa (including isolated USH2A disease)
Age-related or noise-induced high-frequency sensorineural loss with coincidental retinopathy
Mitochondrial syndromes combining hearing loss and retinal degeneration
Bardet-Biedl and other ciliopathies with retinal and sensory features
additionalInvestigations: Pure-tone audiometry documenting the sloping high-frequency sensorineural loss
Optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence for retinal monitoring
Visual field perimetry to track peripheral constriction
Molecular genetic testing prioritising USH2A, then ADGRV1 and WHRN
Assessment of speech and language development with hearing-aid benefit
redFlags: New night blindness or peripheral field loss in an adolescent with congenital hearing loss
Documented progression of hearing thresholds suggesting a more severe course
Rapidly constricting visual fields affecting mobility or driving
Family history of combined hearing and visual loss in siblings
Central visual acuity decline indicating macular involvement
reference.prognosis: Hearing loss is generally stable and well managed with hearing aids, while retinitis pigmentosa progresses more slowly than in type 1; useful central vision is often retained into mid-adulthood before significant field loss. Overall visual and functional outlook is better than type 1.
pitfalls: Labelling the retinopathy as non-syndromic and missing the associated hearing component (or vice versa)
Assuming the hearing loss is progressive and prematurely recommending cochlear implantation
Overlooking early retinitis pigmentosa because vision seems adequate in youth
Failing to test relatives given the shared USH2A basis of isolated retinitis pigmentosa
Confusing the later visual onset with a benign prognosis and omitting low-vision planning
